new_statements.quote: L’accent de mot est un accent démarcatif, qui permet de segmenter la chaîne parlée et de repérer les unités. [...] L’accent tonique primaire tombe sur la syllabe pénultième, dont il augmente l’intensité, rallonge la durée de la voyelle, et élève légèrement la hauteur. Il est accompagné, dans les mots de quatre syllabes au moins, par un accent tonique secondaire [...] L’accent primaire frappe normalement la voyelle pénultième, et n’a pas de valeur contrastive. Un accent secondaire frappe également la première syllabe pour les mots de quatre syllabes ou plus, indépendamment du nombre de syllabes qui la sépare de la syllabe pénultième tonique.
new_statements.translation: Word accent is a demarcative accent, which makes it possible to segment the speech chain and locate the units. [...] Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable, whose intensity it increases, whose vowel it lengthens, and whose pitch it raises slightly. In words of at least four syllables it is accompanied by a secondary stress [...] Primary stress normally falls on the penultimate vowel and has no contrastive value. A secondary stress also falls on the first syllable of words of four or more syllables, regardless of the number of syllables separating it from the stressed penultimate syllable.

Both quoted passages are there verbatim: 'L'accent de mot est un accent démarcatif, qui permet de segmenter la chaîne parlée et de repérer les unités.'.. Il est accompagné, dans les mots de quatre syllabes au moins, par un accent tonique secondaire'.. 'L'accent primaire frappe normalement la voyelle pénultième, et n'a pas de valeur contrastive. Un accent secondaire frappe également la première syllabe pour les mots…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word, counted from the right end of the word including suffixes (suffixation shifts the stress: ['sawa] 'dance' vs [sa'wana] 'the dance', ['nia] 'bed' vs [ni'aku] 'my bed'), whereas enclitics are outside the domain and leave the host's stress in place (p. 64, Tableau 1). Stress is non-contrastive and demarcative; vowel sequences are separate syllables ([mba'tau] 'breadfruit'), which is how the penult rule is established (p. 36).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of words of four or more syllables, whatever the distance to the penult: ["mbamba'rau] 'long', ["tau'nixi] 'hide', ["taf(a)ra'xata] 'get up', ["tamara'xai] 'old man' (Tableau 8, p. 55); in 5-syllable ma-prefixed CVC-reduplicated forms the secondary stress falls on the reduplicated (second) syllable instead: ["makorko'roma], ["makwirkwi'rina] (p. 55).
new_statements.exceptions: Words ending in [aj]/[ej] are phonetically stressed on the last syllable (["tamara'xaj] 'old man', [roro'kʷaj] 'hot') because the final /i/ is realised as a glide and does not count as a syllable; when a word loses its final vowel by sandhi, stress moves left so as to stay on the penult (p. 37). ma-reduplicated 5-syllable forms (above). Footnote 13 (p. 54) notes that the Manam/Fijian antepenult-attraction rule may be POc, in which case Sun̄wadia is not an exact POc reflex.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological/accentual word ('mot phonologique et accentuel', p. 53): affixes are inside, clitics are separate words that take their own penult stress. Henri states there is no phrase accent; a separate contrastive/emphatic accent (vowel lengthening + falling-rising intonation) and sentence intonation peaks on the stressed penult of the focal constituent are described on pp. 55-56. Statement is based on two field trips (Naone village, north Maewo) with recorded corpus; no instrumental study. On the identity of the variety: this statement is for Sun̄wadia (North Maewo, Glottolog mari1426 / ISO mrb), a sister language of Central Maewo, not for cent2058 itself.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is NOT for cent2058. Henri 2011 describes Sun̄wadia, the language of the northern tip of Maewo (villages Naone, Marino/Lelevia, Naumumu; c. 500 speakers), which Glottolog files as mari1426 'Sunwadia' (ISO mrb 'Marino'); Henri herself contrasts it with 'le sun̄wadaga (Central Maewo)' (p. 24) and says no Maewo language had been described before her work (p. 26). Lynch & Crowley 2001 (§3.5.5) record Sun̄wadaga (Central Maewo) as having no phonology and no grammar, only Tryon's 1976 Peterara wordlist. So for cent2058 proper, every accessible description Glottolog assigns to it (Ivens 1940 Lotora; Codrington 1885 Tanoriki; Ray 1926) is silent on stress, and note that Lynch & Crowley 2001 and Henri 2011 assign those Lotora/Tanoriki materials to North Maewo (mari1426) anyway. Recommendation: file the Henri 2011 penult statement under mari1426 (which the earlier scan marked the named source could not be reached; the PDF is open on HAL and now obtained by the project in this directory), and leave cent2058 without a first-hand statement. Wikipedia's 'Sungwadaga language' page copies Henri's phonology onto Sungwadaga; do not follow it.

sources.note: Glottolog cent2058 meds: Ivens 1940 (grammar sketch) and Codrington 1885 only; dialects Lotora, Peterara, Tanoriki. Glottolog mari1426 meds: Henri 2011 (full grammar, 463 pp.), Henri 2010 thesis, Tryon 1976. Grambank coded cent2058 from Ivens 1940 alone. ABVD Sungwadaga (Roŋnawo) wordlist (Rodriguez & Ennever 2018) carries no stress marks. Henri's thesis is not online at theses.fr. Wikipedia 'Sungwadaga language' copies its phonology from Henri 2011 (i.e. from Sungwadia) — an identity conflation.
